questions.question: Is it good to honour the bones and belongings of saints, keeping them in churches and venerating them?

sides.summary: Relics are not worshipped as gods; the ceremony that was idolatry when done for idols is right when done to honour martyrs.
sides.quote: In the one case respect was paid to idols, and therefore the ceremony is to be abhorred; in the other the martyrs are venerated, and the same ceremony is therefore to be allowed.
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: Kissing relics and lighting tapers before them is a heathen custom brought into the church. His book is lost; Jerome quotes it in order to attack it.
sides.quote: Under the cloak of religion we see what is all but a heathen ceremony introduced into the churches: while the sun is still shining, heaps of tapers are lighted, and everywhere a paltry bit of powder, wrapped up in a costly cloth, is kissed and worshipped.
sides.work: Against Vigilantius (Jerome quoting Vigilantius's lost pamphlet)
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6
sides.note: Vigilantius (fl. c. 400, presbyter in Gaul) is known only through Jerome, a hostile reporter; not in the candidate pool.

sides.summary: Rebuked the Egyptian custom of keeping holy bodies above ground in houses, and ordered his own grave hidden so no one could honour his body.
sides.quote: Bury my body, therefore, and hide it underground yourselves, and let my words be observed by you that no one may know the place but you alone. For at the resurrection of the dead I shall receive it incorruptible from the Saviour.
sides.translation: H. Ellershaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 4
sides.note: Antony objected to keeping bodies unburied in homes, not to honouring martyrs as such. Athanasius knew him personally.

questions.splits_people_today: Splits cleanly: Catholics and Orthodox honour relics; most Protestants and most non-religious people find the practice strange or wrong. The split among the Fathers is lopsided (almost all honoured relics), so the pool will mostly sit on one side.
questions.quiz_fit: Good as a plain statement ("Honouring the bones of saints is a good Christian practice"). Denominationally loaded, so it tells more about church background than character. Vigilantius is a vivid farthest-match but is not in the pool.

questions.question: Can people who have died and are with God pray for us?

sides.summary: If apostles and martyrs could pray for others while alive, they can do so much more after winning their crowns.
sides.quote: If Apostles and martyrs while still in the body can pray for others, when they ought still to be anxious for themselves, how much more must they do so when once they have won their crowns, overcome, and triumphed?
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: Prayer for one another is for this life only; after death no one's prayer for another is heard. Known only through Jerome's hostile report.
sides.quote: You say, in your pamphlet, that so long as we are alive we can pray for one another; but once we die, the prayer of no person for another can be heard
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: The dead do not see what happens here as it happens; they learn of it later from new arrivals or from angels. Elsewhere he holds that God works through the martyrs.
sides.quote: So then we must confess that the dead indeed do not know what is doing here, but while it is in doing here: afterwards, however, they hear it from those who from hence go to them at their death
sides.work: On the Care to be Had for the Dead
sides.translation: H. Browne, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 3

questions.splits_people_today: Splits along church lines (Catholic and Orthodox yes; most Protestants no). Many unchurched people also like the idea of a dead grandparent "watching over" them, so it is less one-sided than it looks.
questions.quiz_fit: Workable in plain words ("People in heaven can pray for us"). Augustine's nuance (they do not see us directly) is a nice reveal.

questions.question: Does it help to pray for people who have died?

sides.summary: The souls of the dead are helped by the Eucharist and alms offered for them, though only those whose lives made them able to be helped.
sides.quote: Nor can it be denied that the souls of the dead are benefited by the piety of their living friends, who offer the sacrifice of the Mediator, or give alms in the church on their behalf.
sides.translation: J. F. Shaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 3

sides.summary: Dying, she asked only to be remembered at the altar.
sides.quote: Lay this body anywhere, let not the care for it trouble you at all. This only I ask, that you will remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be.
sides.work: Confessions (Augustine reporting his mother's dying words)
sides.translation: J. G. Pilkington, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1
sides.note: Not in the pool; a direct report by her son, who was present.

sides.summary: A faithful widow prays for her husband's soul and offers for him on the anniversary of his death.
sides.quote: Indeed, she prays for his soul, and requests refreshment for him meanwhile, and fellowship (with him) in the first resurrection; and she offers (her sacrifice) on the anniversaries of his falling asleep.
sides.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4

sides.summary: The apostles themselves ordered the dead to be remembered at the Eucharist, and it brings them great gain.
sides.quote: Not in vain did the Apostles order that remembrance should be made of the dead in the dreadful Mysteries. They know that great gain results to them, great benefit;
sides.translation: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 13

sides.summary: Taught that the offering should not be made for the dead. His own writings are lost; the view is reported by Epiphanius and, after him, Augustine.
sides.quote: [Aerius taught,] saying that the offering ought not to be made for those who have fallen asleep.
sides.work: Augustine, On Heresies (De haeresibus), reporting Aerius
sides.translation: own rendering; Latin text: augustinus.it (Nuova Biblioteca Agostiniana, following the Maurist edition)
sides.heterodox: Judged a heretic (also Arian, per Augustine).
sides.note: Not in the pool. Epiphanius, Panarion 75, is the fuller report, in Greek.
sides.original: dicens offerri pro dormientibus non oportere

questions.splits_people_today: Splits clearly: Catholics and Orthodox pray for the dead; most Protestants do not; many non-religious people light candles or "send thoughts" and would lean yes.
questions.quiz_fit: Strong plain statement ("Praying for people who have died can help them"). The Fathers are nearly all on one side, so it separates the player from the pool more than it separates Fathers from each other.

questions.question: Should babies be baptized?

sides.summary: Delay of baptism is better, especially for little children.
sides.quote: And so, according to the circumstances and disposition, and even age, of each individual, the delay of baptism is preferable; principally, however, in the case of little children.
sides.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 3

sides.summary: Let children come to Christ as they grow up and learn, and become Christians when they can know Him.
sides.quote: Let them come, then, while they are growing up; let them come while they are learning, while they are learning whither to come; let them become Christians when they have become able to know Christ.
sides.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 3

sides.summary: His council of 66 bishops rejected waiting even until the eighth day: grace is not to be refused to anyone born.
sides.quote: we all rather judge that the mercy and grace of God is not to be refused to any one born of man.
sides.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 5

sides.summary: Baptize a child at once if in danger; otherwise wait until about three, when the child can answer a little.
sides.quote: But in respect of others I give my advice to wait till the end of the third year, or a little more or less, when they may be able to listen and to answer something about the Sacrament;
sides.translation: C. G. Browne and J. E. Swallow, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 7

questions.splits_people_today: A real and live split: Catholics, Orthodox, Anglicans, Lutherans, Methodists and Presbyterians baptize infants; Baptists, Pentecostals and most non-denominational churches do not. Non-religious people often have a view (a choice the child should make).
questions.quiz_fit: Very good. Plain, personal, and the Fathers genuinely split three ways (Tertullian no, Cyprian yes at once, Gregory wait a little).

questions.question: If someone was baptized in a group that got the faith wrong, should they be baptized again when they join the true church?

sides.summary: Baptism outside the Church is no baptism; converts are not re-baptized but baptized for the first time.
sides.quote: deciding that there is one baptism which is appointed in the Catholic Church; and that by this those are not re-baptized, but baptized by us, who at any time come from the adulterous and unhallowed water to be washed and sanctified by the truth of the saving water.
sides.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 5

sides.summary: Against the appeal to custom: custom without truth is only old error.
sides.quote: for custom without truth is the antiquity of error.
sides.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 5

sides.summary: Innovate nothing: receive such converts by the laying on of hands for repentance, not a new baptism. Known from Cyprian's quotation of his letter.
sides.quote: If any one, therefore, come to you from any heresy whatever, let nothing be innovated (or done) which has not been handed down, to wit, that hands be imposed on him for repentance;
sides.work: Letter of Stephen, quoted by Cyprian in Epistle 73 (74), to Pompey
sides.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 5

sides.summary: Those who rebaptize are guilty of impiety; God's sacraments are real even when given in schism.
sides.quote: And hence it is clear that they are guilty of impiety who endeavor to rebaptize those who are in Catholic unity; and we act rightly who do not dare to repudiate God's sacraments, even when administered in schism.
sides.translation: J. R. King, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 4

questions.splits_people_today: Splits among churchgoers: Baptists and many free churches rebaptize people baptized as infants or in other traditions; Catholics and most Protestants do not; Orthodox practice varies. Most non-religious people have no view.
questions.quiz_fit: Middling. Real and well documented (Cyprian vs Augustine is a clean pool-vs-pool clash), but the wording needs care to stay plain. Could be "If you were baptized in another church, you should be baptized again in mine."

questions.question: Do pictures of Jesus and the saints belong in church?

sides.summary: Pictures teach those who cannot read; do not destroy them, but forbid their adoration.
sides.quote: For pictorial representation is made use of in Churches for this reason; that such as are ignorant of letters may at least read by looking at the walls what they cannot read in books.
sides.translation: J. Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 13

sides.summary: Broke the images in his churches because people were adoring them. Known from Gregory's rebuke.
sides.quote: you had broken images of saints, as though under the plea that they ought not to be adored
sides.work: Gregory the Great, Letters, to Serenus
sides.translation: J. Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 13

sides.summary: Tore down a church curtain bearing an image of Christ or a saint as against Scripture.
sides.quote: Seeing this, and being loth that an image of a man should be hung up in Christ's church contrary to the teaching of the Scriptures, I tore it asunder and advised the custodians of the place to use it as a winding sheet for some poor person.
sides.work: Letter to John of Jerusalem (Jerome's Latin version, Jerome Letter 51)
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6
sides.note: Not in the pool. Some scholars have questioned whether section 9 is original, but it stands in Jerome's Latin of 394, long before the iconoclast controversy.

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches use images; Reformed and many evangelical churches avoid them; most non-religious people see no harm in art.
questions.quiz_fit: Good and plain. Gregory the Great (pool) against Epiphanius (not pool) is a strong contrast; the pool itself is mostly pro-image.

questions.question: Did Mary have other children after Jesus?

sides.summary: Mary remained a virgin after the birth; the "brothers" were cousins or kin.
sides.quote: And I must also entreat God the Father to show that the mother of His Son, who was a mother before she was a bride, continued a Virgin after her son was born.
sides.work: Against Helvidius (The Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary)
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: Joseph "knew her not till" she bore a son, so she was known afterwards. Known only through Jerome.
sides.quote: It is clear, says he, that she was known after she brought forth, and that that knowledge was only delayed by her engendering a son.
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: Mary was a virgin at Christ's birth and married once for all afterwards (so a wife, not a lifelong virgin).
sides.quote: And indeed it was a virgin, about to marry once for all after her delivery, who gave birth to Christ, in order that each title of sanctity might be fulfilled in Christ's parentage, by means of a mother who was both virgin, and wife of one husband.
sides.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4
sides.note: Helvidius cited Tertullian as his witness; Jerome replied that Tertullian "did not belong to the Church".

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: Catholics and Orthodox (and Luther, Calvin, Wesley) held perpetual virginity; most modern Protestants and most non-religious readers of the Gospels assume Mary had more children.
questions.quiz_fit: Plain and people do have opinions. Doctrinal rather than about how to live. Tertullian vs Jerome is a clean pool contrast.

questions.question: Should priests and pastors be free to marry and live as married men?

sides.summary: The Eastern, Egyptian and Roman churches rightly accept only virgins, the continent, or married men who give up married relations.
sides.quote: What is to become of the Egyptian Churches and those belonging to the Apostolic Seat, which accept for the ministry only men who are virgins, or those who practice continency, or, if married, abandon their conjugal rights?
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: Jerome reports that bishops who agreed with him ordained only men already married.
sides.quote: who ordain no deacons but such as have been previously married; who credit no celibate with chastity
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6
sides.note: Not in the pool; hostile report.

sides.summary: At Nicaea urged the bishops not to forbid married clergy their wives, calling married intercourse chastity.
sides.quote: 'For all men,' said he, 'cannot bear the practice of rigid continence; neither perhaps would the chastity of the wife of each be preserved': and he termed the intercourse of a man with his lawful wife chastity.
sides.translation: A. C. Zenos, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 2
sides.note: Not in the pool. Socrates wrote about a century after Nicaea; some historians doubt the episode.

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: Catholics (Latin rite) require celibate priests; Orthodox ordain married men; Protestants let pastors marry. Many Catholics themselves would allow it. Non-religious people mostly say yes.
questions.quiz_fit: Plain and opinionated. Pool coverage is thin on the "agree" side (the named supporters are outside the pool).

questions.question: If your spouse cheats on you and you divorce, are you free to marry someone else?

sides.summary: Put away an adulterous wife but remain single, so that she can return if she repents.
sides.quote: The husband should put her away, and remain by himself. But if he put his wife away and marry another, he also commits adultery.
sides.translation: F. Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 2
sides.note: Not in the pool (Rome, second century).

sides.summary: A woman who left an adulterous husband and remarried while he lived is an adulteress.
sides.quote: The apostle has thus cut away every plea and has clearly declared that, if a woman marries again while her husband is living, she is an adulteress.
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: The Lord's rule binds men and women alike, but church custom treats them differently; an abandoned husband who remarries is pardonable.
sides.quote: But the man who has been abandoned is pardonable, and the woman who lives with such a man is not condemned.
sides.translation: B. Jackson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 8

sides.summary: A wife may not be put away except for adultery, and the bond is never dissolved unless unfaithfulness has broken it. He does not spell out remarriage.
sides.quote: On this account He has commanded that the wife shall not be put away unless convicted of adultery, and that the bond of the conjugal compact shall never be dissolved, unless unfaithfulness have broken it.
sides.translation: W. Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 7

sides.summary: In 413 he judged Scripture so obscure on a man who divorces an adulteress and remarries that anyone mistaken there errs pardonably. Later (On Adulterous Marriages, c. 419) he held such remarriage to be adultery.
sides.quote: In the divine sayings themselves it is so obscure whether this man too, who is without doubt allowed to put away an adulteress, is still to be held an adulterer if he marries another, that, as far as I can judge, anyone who is mistaken here is mistaken pardonably.
sides.work: On Faith and Works (De fide et operibus)
sides.translation: own rendering; Latin text: augustinus.it (Nuova Biblioteca Agostiniana, following the Maurist edition)
sides.original: in ipsis divinis sententiis ita obscurum est utrum et iste, cui quidem sine dubio adulteram licet dimittere, adulter tamen habeatur si alteram duxerit, ut, quantum existimo, venialiter ibi quisque fallatur.

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: Catholic teaching says no; most Protestants and the Orthodox (by concession) say yes; almost all non-religious people say yes.
questions.quiz_fit: Good and personal, but sensitive for divorced players; word it gently. The Fathers split three ways, which is ideal.

questions.question: After a husband or wife dies, is it right for the one left behind to marry again?

sides.summary: No sin in marrying again, though staying single wins greater honour.
sides.quote: There is no sin in marrying again, said he; but if they remain unmarried, they gain greater honour and glory with the Lord; but if they marry, they do not sin.
sides.translation: F. Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 2

sides.summary: Second marriages are not condemned, only set in lower honour; he rebukes Tertullian by name for attacking them.
sides.quote: which Tertullian also, inflated with cheeks full of sound not of wisdom, while with railing tooth he attacks second marriages, as though unlawful, which the Apostle with sober mind allows to be altogether lawful.
sides.translation: C. L. Cornish, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 3

sides.summary: As a Montanist: one marriage only, as there is one God.
sides.quote: We admit one marriage, just as we do one God.
sides.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4
sides.heterodox: Montanist period; earlier, in To His Wife, he only advised against it.

sides.summary: A second marriage is only a respectable-looking adultery.
sides.quote: for a second marriage is only a specious adultery.
sides.translation: B. P. Pratten, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: One-sided today: almost everyone, religious or not, thinks a widow or widower may remarry. The Fathers were genuinely split.
questions.quiz_fit: Excellent "who would argue with you" item: nearly every player agrees, and Tertullian becomes a memorable farthest match. Weak at telling players apart.

questions.question: Should a Christian only marry another Christian?

sides.summary: Believers who marry pagans commit fornication and should be cut off from the brethren.
sides.quote: it is certain that believers contracting marriages with Gentiles are guilty of fornication, and are to be excluded from all communication with the brotherhood
sides.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4

sides.summary: Lists marriage with unbelievers among the sins that brought persecution on the church.
sides.quote: They united in the bond of marriage with unbelievers; they prostituted the members of Christ to the Gentiles.
sides.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 5

sides.summary: Notes that such marriages are no longer thought sins in his day, since the New Testament gives no command about them; the matter is treated as allowed or left open.
sides.quote: ...which in our times are no longer thought to be sins; for in truth nothing has been commanded about it in the New Testament, and so it has either been believed to be allowed, or left as a doubtful matter.
sides.work: On Faith and Works (De fide et operibus)
sides.translation: own rendering; Latin text: augustinus.it (Nuova Biblioteca Agostiniana, following the Maurist edition)
sides.note: Augustine is reporting the practice of his day and citing Cyprian against it; he does not himself commend such marriages.
sides.original: quae nostris temporibus iam non putantur esse peccata; quoniam revera in Novo Testamento nihil inde praeceptum est, et ideo aut licere creditum est, aut velut dubium derelictum.

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: many committed Christians (and Muslims, and observant Jews) hold to marrying within the faith; many nominal Christians and most non-religious people see it as a private matter.
questions.quiz_fit: Very good. Everyday, personal, and not obviously about Scripture.

questions.question: Is sex within marriage good even when a couple is not trying to have children?

sides.summary: Intercourse for any purpose other than begetting children does injury to nature. (The ANF left this chapter in Latin.)
sides.quote: To come together for any other purpose than the begetting of children is to do injury to nature.
sides.translation: own rendering of the Latin version printed in Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 2 (Clement wrote in Greek)
sides.original: Aliter autem coire, quam ad liberorum procreationem, est facere injuriam naturæ

sides.summary: Intercourse for children has no fault; for pleasure within marriage it is a pardonable (venial) fault.
sides.quote: For intercourse of marriage for the sake of begetting has not fault; but for the satisfying of lust, but yet with husband or wife, by reason of the faith of the bed, it has venial fault:
sides.translation: C. L. Cornish, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 3

sides.summary: Even without a child, a couple's coming together makes them one, like ointment mixed into oil.
sides.quote: What then? When there is no child, will they not be two? Nay, for their coming together has this effect, it diffuses and commingles the bodies of both. And as one who has cast ointment into oil, has made the whole one; so in truth is it also here.
sides.translation: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 13

questions.splits_people_today: One-sided today: nearly everyone, including most Christians, says yes. A small minority (some traditionalists) hold the older view.
questions.quiz_fit: Frank but strong as a "which would argue with you" item. May be too intimate for a light quiz; the owner should decide.

questions.question: Is the state ever right to put a criminal to death?

sides.summary: Killing is always forbidden, so a Christian may not even bring a capital charge.
sides.quote: nor to accuse any one of a capital charge, because it makes no difference whether you put a man to death by word, or rather by the sword, since it is the act of putting to death itself which is prohibited.
sides.translation: W. Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 7

sides.summary: Christians cannot bear even to see a man put to death, though justly.
sides.quote: For when they know that we cannot endure even to see a man put to death, though justly
sides.translation: B. P. Pratten, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 2

sides.summary: Accepts that the state may execute, yet begged a Christian judge to punish even the killers of a priest without taking their lives.
sides.quote: our desire is rather that justice be satisfied without the taking of their lives or the maiming of their bodies in any part
sides.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1
sides.note: For the principle see City of God 1.21: those who "represented in their persons the public justice... and in this capacity have put to death wicked men" have not violated the commandment.

sides.summary: The principle: killing by public authority under law is not murder.
sides.quote: they who have waged war in obedience to the divine command, or in conformity with His laws, have represented in their persons the public justice or the wisdom of government, and in this capacity have put to death wicked men; such persons have by no means violated the commandment, You shall not kill.
sides.translation: M. Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: A real split: roughly half of Americans support the death penalty; most Europeans oppose it; Christians are divided (recent popes oppose it; many evangelicals support it).
questions.quiz_fit: Very good. Plain, contested today, and the pool splits (Lactantius no, Augustine yes-but-spare-them). Overlaps "war" only slightly.

questions.question: May a Christian kill an attacker to save their own life?

sides.summary: A Christian may not save his life by another's death; even facing an armed robber he may not strike back.
sides.quote: I do not think that a Christian, a just and a wise man, ought to save his own life by the death of another; just as when he meets with an armed robber he cannot return his blows, lest in defending his life he should stain his love toward his neighbour.
sides.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
sides.translation: H. de Romestin, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 10

sides.summary: He does not approve killing to defend one's own life, unless one is a soldier or official acting for others.
sides.quote: As to killing others in order to defend one's own life, I do not approve of this, unless one happen to be a soldier or public functionary acting, not for himself, but in defense of others or of the city in which he resides
sides.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1

questions.splits_people_today: Mostly one-sided today: most people, Christian or not, think lethal self-defence is justified; a minority (Anabaptists, Quakers, strict pacifists) disagree.
questions.quiz_fit: Excellent "who would argue with you" item: most players agree, and Ambrose and Augustine both disagree, which surprises. One-sided among the Fathers found, so it discriminates players from Fathers rather than Fathers from each other. Overlaps "war" a little.

questions.question: Is it wrong for a Christian to swear an oath, even in court?

sides.summary: Christ forbade oaths; "necessity" is no excuse where the law is broken.
sides.quote: But what, says one, if it be necessary to take an oath? Where there is a transgression of the law, there is no such thing as necessity.
sides.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 9

sides.summary: Swearing is not good but can be necessary, when people will not otherwise believe what they need to; avoid it as far as you can.
sides.quote: And therefore let him who understands that swearing is to be reckoned not among things that are good, but among things that are necessary, refrain as far as he can from indulging in it, unless by necessity, when he sees men slow to believe what it is useful for them to believe, except they be assured by an oath.
sides.work: Our Lord's Sermon on the Mount
sides.translation: W. Findlay, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 6

questions.splits_people_today: Mostly one-sided: nearly everyone thinks oaths in court are fine; Quakers, Mennonites and some others refuse and "affirm" instead.
questions.quiz_fit: Good "argue with you" item with a clean pool-vs-pool split (Chrysostom vs Augustine). Plain wording: "It is fine for a Christian to swear an oath in court."

questions.question: Is it better for a Christian not to drink alcohol at all?

sides.summary: Do not blame wine for drunkenness: wine is God's work, drunkenness the devil's.
sides.quote: We should say then in answer to such, Let there be no drunkenness; for wine is the work of God, but drunkenness is the work of the devil.
sides.translation: W. R. W. Stephens, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 9

sides.summary: Admires those who shun wine and keeps the young from it, while allowing moderate use to older people.
sides.quote: I therefore admire those who have adopted an austere life, and who are fond of water, the medicine of temperance, and flee as far as possible from wine, shunning it as they would the danger of fire.
sides.translation: W. Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: many Baptists, Pentecostals, Methodists of the older kind, Muslims and health-minded people abstain; most Catholics, Orthodox, Lutherans, Anglicans and non-religious people drink in moderation.
questions.quiz_fit: Good, everyday and plain. Pool coverage is two-sided only in degree; Tatian and the Encratites (who refused wine) are the true opposite, but their own words survive only in hostile reports.

questions.question: When you are ill, is going to the doctor fully in keeping with trusting God?

sides.summary: Medicine is God's gift like farming or weaving; use it without putting all your hope in it. Refusing it outright is contentious.
sides.quote: While to avoid entirely the benefit of medicine shows a contentious spirit.
sides.translation: W. K. L. Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK, 1925)
sides.note: Page is an OCR text of the 1925 book; the sentence quoted is clean.

sides.summary: The sick may take the ordinary road of medicine, or the higher and better road of seeking God through prayer.
sides.quote: But in seeking recovery from disease, a man must either follow the more ordinary and simple method, and have recourse to medical art; or if he would go beyond the common methods adopted by men, he must rise to the higher and better way of seeking the blessing of Him who is God over all, through piety and prayers.
sides.translation: F. Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4
sides.heterodox: Some of his views were condemned in 553.

sides.summary: Medicine belongs with the pagan arts; whoever is healed by trusting matter would be healed better by turning to God.
sides.quote: But medicine and everything included in it is an invention of the same kind. If any one is healed by matter, through trusting to it, much more will he be healed by having recourse to the power of God.
sides.translation: J. E. Ryland, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 2
sides.heterodox: Later founded or joined the Encratites; judged a heretic by Irenaeus.

questions.splits_people_today: Mostly one-sided: almost everyone says yes. A small minority (some faith-healing groups, Christian Scientists) say no. Many people feel a quieter version of the tension ("should I pray first?").
questions.quiz_fit: Good as an "argue with you" item and a fun reveal (Basil, who founded a hospital, calls refusal "contentious"). Tatian is outside the pool.

questions.question: Is a lot of laughter a good thing in a Christian life?

sides.summary: Church is not a theatre for laughter; Christ is often seen weeping but never laughing. He says he does not forbid all laughter, only dissipation.
sides.quote: For this is not the theatre for laughter, neither did we come together for this intent, that we may give way to immoderate mirth, but that we may groan, and by this groaning inherit a kingdom.
sides.translation: G. Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 10

sides.summary: Rule 17 of the Longer Rules: refrain from loud laughter; a cheerful smile is enough.
sides.quote: THAT IT IS NECESSARY ALSO TO REFRAIN FROM LAUGHTER
sides.translation: W. K. L. Clarke, The Ascetic Works of Saint Basil (SPCK, 1925)

sides.summary: Laughter is natural and must not be rooted out, only kept within limits and times; pleasantry yes, clowning no.
sides.quote: For, in a word, whatever things are natural to men we must not eradicate from them, but rather impose on them limits and suitable times.
sides.translation: W. Wilson, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: One-sided today: nearly everyone thinks laughter is healthy and good.
questions.quiz_fit: Strong "which would argue with you" item: Chrysostom as the farthest match on laughter is memorable and a little funny. Overlaps "emotions" and "enjoyment" slightly.

questions.question: Is it fine for Christians to keep holidays and customs that began as pagan ones, giving them new meaning?

sides.summary: Christians keep the Saturnalia, New Year and Midwinter feasts with gifts and banquets, while pagans would never keep a Christian feast.
sides.quote: By us, to whom Sabbaths are strange, and the new moons and festivals formerly beloved by God, the Saturnalia and New-year's and Midwinter's festivals and Matronalia are frequented — presents come and go — New-year's gifts — games join their noise — banquets join their din!
sides.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 3

sides.summary: Do not destroy the English temples or feasts; turn them into churches and Christian festivals, since hard hearts climb by steps.
sides.quote: For it is undoubtedly impossible to cut away everything at once from hard hearts, since one who strives to ascend to the highest place must needs rise by steps or paces, and not by leaps.
sides.translation: J. Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 13

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: most Christians happily keep Christmas trees and Halloween; some (Jehovah's Witnesses, some Reformed and Messianic groups, "pagan origins" critics) refuse.
questions.quiz_fit: Very good. Everyday, fun, and a clean pool-vs-pool clash (Tertullian vs Gregory the Great).

questions.question: Is the end of the world probably near, within our lifetimes or soon after?

sides.summary: Told King Ethelbert that the end of the present world was already close at hand.
sides.quote: the end of the present world is already close at hand, and the reign of the saints is coming, which can have no end.
sides.work: Letters, to Ethelbert (Edilbert), King of the Angles
sides.translation: J. Barmby, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 13

sides.summary: The world has grown old and lost its strength.
sides.quote: that the world has now grown old, and does not abide in that strength in which it formerly stood; nor has it that vigour and force which it formerly possessed.
sides.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 5

sides.summary: The six thousand years are nearly complete; at most two hundred years remain.
sides.quote: yet all expectation does not exceed the limit of two hundred years.
sides.translation: W. Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 7

sides.summary: Christ silenced the calculators: it is not for us to know the times.
sides.quote: But on this subject He puts aside the figures of the calculators, and orders silence, who says, It is not for you to know the times, which the Father has put in His own power.
sides.translation: M. Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: a large minority of American Christians expect Christ's return within decades; many others, and most non-religious people, do not. Climate and war anxieties give secular people their own version.
questions.quiz_fit: Good, plain, and a real pool split (Gregory the Great and Cyprian vs Augustine).

questions.question: Will Christ return to reign on this earth for a literal thousand years?

sides.summary: He and others expect a thousand years in a rebuilt Jerusalem, while admitting that many true Christians think otherwise.
sides.quote: But I and others, who are right-minded Christians on all points, are assured that there will be a resurrection of the dead, and a thousand years in Jerusalem, which will then be built, adorned, and enlarged, [as] the prophets Ezekiel and Isaiah and others declare.
sides.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 1

sides.summary: The admission that Christians disagreed on this.
sides.quote: I admitted to you formerly, that I and many others are of this opinion, and [believe] that such will take place, as you assuredly are aware; but, on the other hand, I signified to you that many who belong to the pure and pious faith, and are true Christians, think otherwise.
sides.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 1

sides.summary: The righteous must be rewarded in the same creation where they suffered, before the final judgment.
sides.quote: For it is just that in that very creation in which they toiled or were afflicted, being proved in every way by suffering, they should receive the reward of their suffering;
sides.translation: A. Roberts and W. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 1

sides.summary: Once held a spiritual version himself; later taught that the thousand years is the Church's present reign with Christ.
sides.quote: And this opinion would not be objectionable, if it were believed that the joys of the saints in that Sabbath shall be spiritual, and consequent on the presence of God; for I myself, too, once held this opinion.
sides.translation: M. Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 2

sides.summary: His later view: the Church now is the kingdom.
sides.quote: Therefore the Church even now is the kingdom of Christ, and the kingdom of heaven. Accordingly, even now His saints reign with Him, though otherwise than as they shall reign hereafter;
sides.translation: M. Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: Splits among Christians (many American evangelicals are premillennial; Catholics, Orthodox and most mainline Protestants are not). Most non-religious people have no view.
questions.quiz_fit: Real and clean (Justin and Irenaeus vs Augustine, with Augustine's change of mind), but it needs Bible background to answer, so weaker for a general audience.

questions.question: Did your soul exist before you were conceived?

sides.summary: Each being has the causes of its differences in itself, from before its bodily birth.
sides.quote: And this, it appears to me, will be seen more clearly at last, if each one, whether of celestial or terrestrial or infernal beings, be said to have the causes of his diversity in himself, and antecedent to his bodily birth.
sides.translation: F. Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4, from Rufinus's Latin
sides.heterodox: The pre-existence of souls was condemned in 553.
sides.note: The work survives mainly in Rufinus's softened Latin translation.

sides.summary: Soul and body begin together; man is one and cannot be earlier and later than himself.
sides.quote: But as man is one, the being consisting of soul and body, we are to suppose that the beginning of his existence is one, common to both parts, so that he should not be found to be antecedent and posterior to himself, if the bodily element were first in point of time, and the other were a later addition;
sides.translation: H. A. Wilson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 5

questions.splits_people_today: Splits more than expected: Latter-day Saints teach a pre-mortal life; many "spiritual but not religious" people and believers in reincarnation say yes; most Christians say no.
questions.quiz_fit: Good, intriguing to ordinary people, and a clean pool-vs-pool split. Origen as nearest match for a New Age player is an honest, striking reveal.

questions.question: Do books like Tobit, Judith, Wisdom and Maccabees belong in the Bible?

sides.summary: The Church reads them for edification but not to settle doctrine; they are not in the canon.
sides.quote: As, then, the Church reads Judith, Tobit, and the books of Maccabees, but does not admit them among the canonical Scriptures, so let it read these two volumes for the edification of the people, not to give authority to doctrines of the Church.
sides.work: Preface to the Books of Solomon
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: Wisdom, Sirach, Esther, Judith and Tobit are outside the canon but appointed to be read by new converts.
sides.quote: that there are other books besides these not indeed included in the Canon, but appointed by the Fathers to be read by those who newly join us, and who wish for instruction in the word of godliness.
sides.translation: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 4

sides.summary: Counts Tobit, Judith, the Maccabees, Wisdom and Sirach among the books of Scripture.
sides.quote: Still they are to be reckoned among the prophetical books, since they have attained recognition as being authoritative.
sides.translation: J. F. Shaw, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: Splits Catholics and Orthodox (yes) from Protestants (no). Most non-religious people and many Christians have never thought about it.
questions.quiz_fit: A clean pool-vs-pool clash, but too specialist for most players. Better as reveal material or an article.

questions.question: Is a Bible translation that changes familiar words worth it if it is closer to the original?

sides.summary: Asked Jerome to translate the familiar Greek Old Testament instead, and reported a town congregation in uproar over one changed word in Jonah.
sides.quote: Thereupon arose such a tumult in the congregation, especially among the Greeks, correcting what had been read, and denouncing the translation as false, that the bishop was compelled to ask the testimony of the Jewish residents (it was in the town of Oea).
sides.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1

sides.summary: His stated preference.
sides.quote: For my part, I would much rather that you would furnish us with a translation of the Greek version of the canonical Scriptures known as the work of the Seventy translators.
sides.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1

sides.summary: Translated from the Hebrew so Latin readers could know the original; no one is forced to read it.
sides.quote: If any one is averse to reading it, none compels him against his will. Let him drink with satisfaction the old wine, and despise my new wine
sides.work: Letter to Augustine (Augustine's Letter 75; Jerome's Letter 112)
sides.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: King James loyalists and many older churchgoers prefer familiar wording; others want the most accurate modern text. The same split exists over updated hymns and liturgies.
questions.quiz_fit: Good and unexpectedly relatable: the Oea "tumult" over one word is a great reveal. Pool-vs-pool (Augustine vs Jerome).

questions.question: Should Christians keep the church's set fast days, like Lent and Fridays?

sides.summary: Fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, not on the days the hypocrites fast.
sides.quote: for they fast on the second and fifth day of the week; but fast on the fourth day and the Preparation (Friday).
sides.work: The Didache (Teaching of the Twelve Apostles)
sides.translation: M. B. Riddle, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 7
sides.note: Anonymous, c. 100; not in the pool.

sides.summary: Fixed fasts should not be kept; fast when you choose, so as not to be under the law. Reported by Augustine after Epiphanius.
sides.quote: ...nor ought the appointed fasts to be solemnly kept; but each should fast when he wishes, lest he seem to be under the law.
sides.work: Augustine, On Heresies (De haeresibus), reporting Aerius
sides.translation: own rendering; Latin text: augustinus.it (Nuova Biblioteca Agostiniana, following the Maurist edition)
sides.original: nec statuta solemniter celebranda esse ieiunia; sed cum quisque voluerit, ieiunandum, ne videatur esse sub lege.

sides.summary: Abstaining from food is no better than eating with thanksgiving. Reported by Jerome.
sides.quote: His third point is that there is no difference between abstinence from food, and its reception with thanksgiving.
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6
sides.heterodox: Condemned at Rome and Milan c. 393.

sides.summary: Scripture commands fasting but fixes no days; follow the custom of your church for peace.
sides.quote: I see that fasting is enjoined. But I do not discover any rule definitely laid down by the Lord or by the apostles as to days on which we ought or ought not to fast.
sides.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: Catholics, Orthodox and many Anglicans keep Lent and fast days; most evangelicals do not, or treat them as optional; non-religious people sometimes adopt "giving something up".
questions.quiz_fit: Decent. Plain enough, but overlaps the "asceticism" topic. The pool members found are Augustine (mixed); the clear "no" voices are outside the pool.

questions.question: Once someone is truly saved, can they never be lost?

sides.summary: Those born again in baptism with full faith cannot be overthrown by the devil; anyone who falls was only baptized with water, not the Spirit. Reported by Jerome.
sides.quote: But if any are tempted, it only shows that they were baptized with water, not with the Spirit, as we read was the case with Simon Magus.
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: The baptized can be tempted and fall by their own free choice; otherwise warnings to add works to faith would be useless.
sides.quote: It was useless to warn them to add works to faith, if they could not sin after baptism.
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: The elect will persevere by God's gift, yet some who truly lived well do fall away by their own will and are justly condemned; no one knows which he is.
sides.quote: we still rebuke those, and reasonably rebuke them, who, although they were living well, have not persevered therein; because they have of their own will been changed from a good to an evil life, and on that account are worthy of rebuke;
sides.translation: P. Holmes and R. E. Wallis, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 5

questions.splits_people_today: Splits Protestants (Baptists and Calvinists often say yes; Methodists, Pentecostals, Catholics and Orthodox say no). Non-religious people rarely have a view.
questions.quiz_fit: Real and heated among Christians; may overlap the "grace-effort" topic. Jovinian as a named nearest match for a Baptist player is interesting but he is outside the pool.

questions.question: Will everyone in heaven receive the same reward?

sides.summary: One reward in heaven for all who kept their baptism. Reported by Jerome.
sides.quote: The fourth and last is that there is one reward in the kingdom of heaven for all who have kept their baptismal vow.
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: God gives each a fitting dwelling, according to their worth (after the elders: thirty-, sixty- and hundredfold).
sides.quote: For all things belong to God, who supplies all with a suitable dwelling-place; even as His Word says, that a share is allotted to all by the Father, according as each person is or shall be worthy.
sides.translation: A. Roberts and W. Rambaut, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 1

sides.summary: There will be degrees of honour, and no one will envy another.
sides.quote: But who can conceive, not to say describe, what degrees of honor and glory shall be awarded to the various degrees of merit? Yet it cannot be doubted that there shall be degrees.
sides.translation: M. Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: Splits quietly: many ordinary believers assume heaven is equal for all; Catholic teaching and many evangelicals ("crowns") hold degrees of reward.
questions.quiz_fit: Middling. Intriguing, but the named "agree" voice is outside the pool.

questions.question: Should churches that keep different customs (like a different date for Easter) still treat each other as one church?

sides.summary: Rebuked Victor of Rome: differing over the fast only confirms agreement in the faith.
sides.quote: Yet all of these lived none the less in peace, and we also live in peace with one another; and the disagreement in regard to the fast confirms the agreement in the faith.
sides.work: Letter to Victor, quoted by Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History
sides.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 1

sides.summary: Held fast to the Asian custom handed down from John: "neither adding, nor taking away".
sides.quote: We observe the exact day; neither adding, nor taking away.
sides.work: Letter to Victor, quoted by Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History
sides.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 1

sides.summary: Tried to cut off all the churches of Asia over the date. Eusebius reports this; Victor's own letter is lost.
sides.quote: Victor, who presided over the church at Rome, immediately attempted to cut off from the common unity the parishes of all Asia, with the churches that agreed with them, as heterodox;
sides.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 1
sides.note: Not in the pool; report, not his words.

sides.summary: On the daily-or-occasional communion dispute: what matters is to stay united in Christ's peace, each free to follow conscience.
sides.quote: reminding them that the principal thing is to remain united in the peace of Christ, and that each should be free to do what, according to his belief, he conscientiously regards as his duty.
sides.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1

questions.splits_people_today: Mostly one-sided in principle (most people say yes), though real churches still divide over practice.
questions.quiz_fit: Weak as a statement (everyone agrees), but the Irenaeus line is excellent reveal copy for a "peacemaker" result.

questions.question: Should you take communion often, even when you feel unworthy?

sides.summary: Confessing ourselves sinners is a reason to hurry to communion for healing, not to stay away; better every Sunday than once a year.
sides.quote: Yet we ought not to suspend ourselves from the Lord's Communion because we confess ourselves sinners, but should more and more eagerly hasten to it for the healing of our soul, and purifying of our spirit,
sides.translation: E. C. S. Gibson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 11

sides.summary: Daily communion is good; he himself received four times a week.
sides.quote: It is good and beneficial to communicate every day, and to partake of the holy body and blood of Christ.
sides.translation: B. Jackson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 8
sides.note: Authenticity of this letter is sometimes questioned.

sides.summary: Complains that people stay away all year and come only at Easter: "there is no one to partake".
sides.quote: In vain is the daily Sacrifice, in vain do we stand before the Altar; there is no one to partake.
sides.translation: Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 13

sides.summary: Both the one who dares not receive daily and the one who dares not miss a day honour the sacrament.
sides.quote: For he that dares not take it every day, and he who dares not omit it any day, are both alike moved by a desire to do it honour.
sides.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1

questions.splits_people_today: Splits among Christians (weekly communion in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Anglican churches; monthly or quarterly in many Protestant ones; "only when worthy" instincts everywhere).
questions.quiz_fit: Middling; church-internal. The "even when you feel unworthy" angle is personal and could work.

questions.question: Would money spent making churches beautiful be better given to the poor?

sides.summary: Melted church vessels to ransom captives: the Church has gold to spend on those in need, not to hoard.
sides.quote: The Church has gold, not to store up, but to lay out, and to spend on those who need.
sides.work: On the Duties of the Clergy
sides.translation: H. de Romestin, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 10

sides.summary: Feed the hungry Christ first, then deck His table; he says he does not forbid gifts to the church.
sides.quote: For what is the profit, when His table indeed is full of golden cups, but He perishes with hunger? First fill Him, being an hungered, and then abundantly deck out His table also.
sides.translation: G. Prevost, rev. M. B. Riddle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 10

sides.summary: In 394: churches glitter with marble and gold while the choice of ministers is neglected. By 414 (Letter 130) he softened: he does not blame builders, but the poor come first for Demetrias.
sides.quote: Many build churches nowadays; their walls and pillars of glowing marble, their ceilings glittering with gold, their altars studded with jewels. Yet to the choice of Christ's ministers no heed is paid.
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.summary: Praised the bishop who built the splendid church at Tyre as a new Bezalel and Solomon.
sides.quote: one might call you a new Beseleel, the architect of a divine tabernacle, or Solomon, king of a new and much better Jerusalem, or also a new Zerubabel, who added a much greater glory than the former to the temple of God;
sides.work: Ecclesiastical History (panegyric on the church at Tyre)
sides.translation: A. C. McGiffert, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 1

questions.splits_people_today: A real split: many people (Christian and not) resent lavish church spending; others defend beauty as worship and as a gift to the poor who cannot afford beauty.
questions.quiz_fit: Good and plain. Overlaps the "wealth" topic, but the church-building angle is distinct.

questions.question: Is it wrong to charge interest when you lend money?

sides.summary: A just man lending money takes no interest; to receive more than he gave is unjust.
sides.quote: If he shall have lent any money, he will not receive interest, that the benefit may be unimpaired which succours necessity, and that he may entirely abstain from the property of another.
sides.translation: W. Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 7

sides.summary: Counts bishops "multiplying usuries" among the sins that brought persecution.
sides.quote: They sought to possess money in hoards, they seized estates by crafty deceits, they increased their gains by multiplying usuries.
sides.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 5

sides.summary: Forbids lending at interest to clergy and laity alike.
sides.quote: For we are grieved that this is practised not only by those who belong to the clergy, but also by laymen who desire to be called Christians.
sides.work: Letter 4, to the bishops of Campania and elsewhere
sides.translation: C. L. Feltoe, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 12

questions.splits_people_today: Mostly one-sided the other way: almost everyone accepts interest on loans and savings, though many condemn payday lending; Islamic finance forbids interest.
questions.quiz_fit: Strong "argue with you" item: the Fathers are unanimous against, most players are not. Does not separate Fathers from each other. Overlaps "wealth" slightly.

questions.question: Is owning another human being always wrong?

sides.summary: To own slaves is to condemn a free human nature to slavery and to legislate against God.
sides.quote: You condemn to slavery a human being, whose nature is free and self-governing, and you make laws against God, overturning His law for human nature.
sides.translation: own rendering of the Greek (Migne, PG 44) as printed at earlychurchtexts.com; modern English versions (S. G. Hall, 1993) are copyrighted
sides.original: Δουλείᾳ καταδικάζεις τὸν ἄνθρωπον, οὗ ἐλευθέρα ἡ φύσις καὶ αὐτεξούσιος, καὶ ἀντινομοθετεῖς τῷ Θεῷ, ἀνατρέπων αὐτοῦ τὸν ἐπὶ τῇ φύσει νόμον.

sides.summary: No one is a slave by nature, but slavery is a just penalty for sin; slaves should serve faithfully until all rule passes away.
sides.quote: But by nature, as God first created us, no one is the slave either of man or of sin. This servitude is, however, penal, and is appointed by that law which enjoins the preservation of the natural order and forbids its disturbance;
sides.translation: M. Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 2

sides.summary: Takes slavery as a fact of church life: do not despise slaves, but let them not seek freedom at the church's expense. He does not argue for or against owning slaves.
sides.quote: Do not despise either male or female slaves, yet neither let them be puffed up with conceit, but rather let them submit themselves the more, for the glory of God, that they may obtain from God a better liberty. Let them not long to be set free [from slavery] at the public expense, that they be not found slaves to their own desires.
sides.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 1

questions.splits_people_today: One-sided today: virtually everyone says yes.
questions.quiz_fit: Poor as a quiz statement (no one disagrees), and risky: it would pin a modern-sounding "wrong" answer on Ignatius or Augustine. Gregory of Nyssa's line is superb reveal or article material.

questions.question: Is it fine for a Christian woman to wear makeup and jewellery?

sides.summary: Rouge and eye-paint censure the Artificer who made the face.
sides.quote: For they who rub their skin with medicaments, stain their cheeks with rouge, make their eyes prominent with antimony, sin against Him
sides.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4

sides.summary: God's workmanship must not be adulterated with dyes, powders or rouge.
sides.quote: that the work of God and His fashioning and formation ought in no manner to be adulterated, either with the application of yellow color, or with black dust or rouge, or with any kind of medicament which can corrupt the native lineaments.
sides.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 5

sides.summary: Do not rush to forbid gold and fine dress to married people, who must please their spouses; but face paint is a dishonest trick.
sides.quote: Let me say, however, in regard to ornaments of gold and costly dress, that I would not have you come to a precipitate decision in the way of forbidding their use, except in the case of those who, neither being married nor intending to marry, are bound to consider only how they may please God.
sides.translation: J. G. Cunningham, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1

questions.splits_people_today: Mostly one-sided: most people, including most Christians, say yes; some conservative groups (Holiness, some Pentecostal and Anabaptist churches) say no.
questions.quiz_fit: Usable as an "argue with you" item, but it addresses women only and could read as scolding; Augustine's split verdict is the interesting reveal.

questions.question: Can your star sign or horoscope tell you something true about your life?

sides.summary: As a young man he consulted astrologers freely; later rejected the art as something Christian piety condemns.
sides.quote: Those impostors, then, whom they designate Mathematicians, I consulted without hesitation, because they used no sacrifices, and invoked the aid of no spirit for their divinations, which art Christian and true piety fitly rejects and condemns.
sides.translation: J. G. Pilkington, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 1

sides.summary: The stars cause nothing, but the heaven may be like a book of God containing things to come, which people cannot read accurately.
sides.quote: But like a book which contains future events in the language of prophecy, it is possible that the whole heaven, being as it were a book of God, may contain the things to come.
sides.work: Commentary on Genesis, quoted by Eusebius, Preparation for the Gospel
sides.translation: E. H. Gifford (1903)

questions.splits_people_today: Splits more than people expect: a large minority, especially younger adults, give horoscopes some credence; most committed Christians and most sceptics do not.
questions.quiz_fit: Good and everyday. Origen's "book of God" line gives a surprising nearest match for a player who half-believes.

questions.question: Is the fire of hell a real, physical fire?

sides.summary: Each sinner kindles his own fire; its fuel is his sins, working like a fever in the soul.
sides.quote: By these words it seems to be indicated that every sinner kindles for himself the flame of his own fire, and is not plunged into some fire which has been already kindled by another, or was in existence before himself.
sides.translation: F. Crombie, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4, from Rufinus's Latin

sides.summary: The risen bodies of the damned will certainly be pained by the fire.
sides.quote: only, this we believe about those future bodies, that they shall be such as shall certainly be pained by the fire.
sides.translation: M. Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: many believers take hell's fire as a picture of separation from God; many others (and older catechisms) take it literally; non-religious people mostly doubt hell altogether.
questions.quiz_fit: Plain and people have views. Overlaps "universal-salvation" only partly (this is about what hell is, not who goes).

questions.question: When careful study of nature clearly shows something, should Christians read the Bible in a way that fits it?

sides.summary: It is shameful and harmful when a non-Christian who knows nature well hears a Christian talk nonsense about it as if from Scripture.
sides.quote: It is a very shameful and harmful thing, and one to be guarded against above all, that [an unbeliever] should hear a Christian, speaking about these things as if according to the Christian Scriptures, talk such nonsense that, seeing him wrong by the whole sky, as the saying goes, he can hardly keep from laughing.
sides.work: The Literal Meaning of Genesis (De Genesi ad litteram)
sides.translation: own rendering; Latin text: augustinus.it (Nuova Biblioteca Agostiniana, following the Maurist edition); the modern English (J. H. Taylor, 1982) is copyrighted
sides.original: Turpe est autem nimis et perniciosum ac maxime cavendum, ut christianum de his rebus quasi secundum christianas Litteras loquentem, ita delirare audiat, ut, quemadmodum dicitur, toto coelo errare conspiciens, risum tenere vix possit.

sides.summary: Mocked the philosophers' round earth: no one could believe in people whose feet are above their heads.
sides.quote: Or is there any one so senseless as to believe that there are men whose footsteps are higher than their heads?
sides.translation: W. Fletcher, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 7
sides.note: His target is pagan natural philosophy rather than a reading of Scripture, so this is a close but not exact match to the question.

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: young-earth creationists put Scripture first; most other Christians and nearly all non-religious people let science inform reading.
questions.quiz_fit: Good and contested. May overlap "creation" or "scripture-sense"; Augustine's line is famous and apt.

questions.question: Should women be allowed to preach and teach in church?

sides.summary: A woman may not speak, teach, baptize or offer in the church.
sides.quote: It is not permitted to a woman to speak in the church; but neither (is it permitted her) to teach, nor to baptize, nor to offer, nor to claim to herself a lot in any manly function, not to say (in any) sacerdotal office.
sides.translation: S. Thelwall, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4

sides.summary: Marcella settled Scripture disputes in Rome, even for priests, but gave her answers as if they were someone else's.
sides.quote: Consequently after my departure from Rome, in case of a dispute arising as to the testimony of scripture on any subject, recourse was had to her to settle it.
sides.translation: W. H. Fremantle, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 6

sides.person: Macrina the Younger (as recorded by her brother Gregory of Nyssa)
sides.summary: Gregory, a bishop, calls his sister Macrina "the Teacher" and records her teaching him on the soul and the resurrection (privately, not in church).
sides.quote: But his sister the Teacher was still living
sides.work: On the Soul and the Resurrection
sides.translation: W. Moore and H. A. Wilson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 5

questions.splits_people_today: A sharp live split: Catholics, Orthodox and many evangelicals say no to women preaching or leading; mainline Protestants and Pentecostals often say yes; most non-religious people say yes.
questions.quiz_fit: Contested and plain, but the Fathers found are one-sided on public teaching; Macrina's example is a good reveal for a nuanced player.

questions.question: Is it fine for Christians to keep Jewish customs like the Sabbath and food laws?

sides.summary: Believers who keep the Mosaic customs without forcing them on others should be welcomed as brethren; some Christians refused, and he disagreed with them.
sides.quote: There are such people, Trypho, and these do not venture to have any intercourse with or to extend hospitality to such persons; but I do not agree with them.
sides.translation: M. Dods and G. Reith, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 1

sides.summary: It is absurd to confess Christ and live like a Jew.
sides.quote: It is absurd to profess Christ Jesus, and to Judaize.
sides.translation: A. Roberts and J. Donaldson, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 1

questions.splits_people_today: Small but real split (Messianic Jews, Seventh-day Adventists, Hebrew Roots groups vs most churches). Most people have no view.
questions.quiz_fit: Weak for a general audience; good historical colour. Justin's tolerance is a nice nuance.

questions.question: Does it matter whether a Christian is buried or cremated?

sides.summary: Christians fear no loss from any kind of burial, but keep the older and better custom of burial in the earth.
sides.quote: Nor, as you believe, do we fear any loss from sepulture, but we adopt the ancient and better custom of burying in the earth.
sides.translation: R. E. Wallis, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 4

sides.summary: Being denied burial does not hurt the faithful; burial is a kindness for the living.
sides.quote: it neither any whit hurts the faithful to have their bodies denied sepulture, nor any whit the giving of sepulture unto infidels advantages them;
sides.work: On the Care to be Had for the Dead
sides.translation: H. Browne, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 3

questions.splits_people_today: Splits: cremation is now common among most Christians and non-religious people; some Orthodox, traditional Catholics, Muslims and Jews prefer burial.
questions.quiz_fit: Middling. The Fathers agree the method harms no one and all prefer burial, so it barely separates them.

questions.question: Is it fine for a Christian to celebrate their own birthday?

sides.summary: No righteous man in Scripture kept a birthday; only Pharaoh and Herod did, and each birthday feast ended in a killing.
sides.quote: Some one of those before us has observed what is written in Genesis about the birthday of Pharaoh, and has told that the worthless man who loves things connected with birth keeps birthday festivals; and we, taking this suggestion from him, find in no Scripture that a birthday was kept by a righteous man.
sides.translation: J. Patrick, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 9 (1896)

questions.splits_people_today: One-sided: almost everyone celebrates birthdays; Jehovah's Witnesses are the well-known exception.
questions.quiz_fit: Fun "argue with you" trivia, but only one Father found (no one else wrote on the question); cannot discriminate between Fathers.

questions.question: Can it ever be right to take your own life?

sides.summary: Virgins who killed themselves to escape rape are counted as martyrs, like St Pelagia.
sides.quote: And indeed as regards virgins placed in the necessity of preserving their purity, we have a plain answer, seeing that there exists an instance of martyrdom.
sides.translation: H. de Romestin, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 10

sides.summary: Scripture gives no command or permission to take one's own life for any reason; a woman violated against her will remains chaste.
sides.quote: It is not without significance, that in no passage of the holy canonical books there can be found either divine precept or permission to take away our own life, whether for the sake of entering on the enjoyment of immortality, or of shunning, or ridding ourselves of anything whatever.
sides.translation: M. Dods, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, First Series (ed. Schaff, 1886-89), vol. 2

questions.splits_people_today: Splits today mainly over assisted dying for the terminally ill.
questions.quiz_fit: Do not use in the quiz: too painful a subject for a playful self-discovery quiz, and the Fathers' case (rape) is not today's case. Recorded for completeness because it is a real Ambrose-Augustine disagreement.

questions.question: Is ending a pregnancy the killing of a human being?

sides.summary: A woman who deliberately destroys her unborn child is a murderer, formed or unformed; penance ten years, not life.
sides.quote: The woman who purposely destroys her unborn child is guilty of murder. With us there is no nice enquiry as to its being formed or unformed.
sides.translation: B. Jackson, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series (ed. Schaff and Wace, 1890-1900), vol. 8

sides.summary: Women who use drugs to cause abortion commit murder.
sides.quote: And when we say that those women who use drugs to bring on abortion commit murder, and will have to give an account to God for the abortion
sides.translation: B. P. Pratten, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 2

sides.summary: Describes surgeons killing a child in the womb to save the mother as a "cruel necessity"; his point is that the unborn child is alive.
sides.quote: But sometimes by a cruel necessity, while yet in the womb, an infant is put to death, when lying awry in the orifice of the womb he impedes parturition, and kills his mother, if he is not to die himself.
sides.translation: P. Holmes, Ante-Nicene Fathers (ed. Roberts and Donaldson, 1885-96), vol. 3

questions.splits_people_today: One of the deepest splits today, religious and political.
questions.quiz_fit: Do not use: politically charged, and the Fathers are essentially unanimous, so it would only mark distance from all of them. Recorded because the evidence is clear.

misattributions.line: Credo quia absurdum ("I believe because it is absurd")
misattributions.truth: Not in Tertullian. The nearest is On the Flesh of Christ 5: "the Son of God died; it is by all means to be believed, because it is absurd. And He was buried, and rose again; the fact is certain, because it is impossible" (ANF 3; newadvent.org/fathers/0315.htm). It is a rhetorical paradox inside an argument against Marcion, not a motto for irrational faith; the Latin tag is a later compression.

misattributions.line: He who is not angry when he has cause to be, sins (and the like: "without anger, teaching will be useless")
misattributions.truth: From the Opus Imperfectum in Matthaeum, homily 11, an anonymous (probably Arian) Latin commentary long circulated under Chrysostom's name. Aquinas quotes it as "Chrysostom" (Summa II-II q.158 a.1); the New Advent edition flags it as "falsely ascribed to St. John Chrysostom".

misattributions.line: The Church is a hospital for sinners, not a museum for saints
misattributions.truth: No source in Augustine or any early Christian writer has been found. It appears in twentieth-century American print. The idea of Christ as physician and the Church as an inn for the wounded (Good Samaritan readings) is patristic; the slogan is not.

misattributions.line: The glory of God is man fully alive
misattributions.truth: A loose paraphrase. Against Heresies 4.20.7 reads: "For the glory of God is a living man; and the life of man consists in beholding God" (ANF 1; newadvent.org/fathers/0103420.htm). The second half, about seeing God, is usually dropped.

misattributions.line: The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church
misattributions.truth: Paraphrase. Apology 50: "The oftener we are mown down by you, the more in number we grow; the blood of Christians is seed" (ANF 3; newadvent.org/fathers/0301.htm).

misattributions.line: Love God and do what you want (as licence)
misattributions.truth: Authentic but bent. Homilies on 1 John 7.8: "Love, and do what you will: whether you hold your peace, through love hold your peace; whether you cry out, through love cry out; whether you correct, through love correct" (NPNF1 7; newadvent.org/fathers/170207.htm). The context is correcting others in love, not permission.

misattributions.line: In essentials unity, in non-essentials liberty, in all things charity
misattributions.truth: Not Augustine. Usually traced to the Lutheran Rupertus Meldenius (Peter Meiderlin), c. 1626. Not verified in this pass beyond secondary knowledge; no patristic source exists.

misattributions.line: Pray as though everything depended on God; work as though everything depended on you
misattributions.truth: Not in Augustine. Usually traced to a Jesuit maxim (Gabriel Hevenesi, 1705) summarising Ignatius of Loyola. Secondary knowledge only; no patristic source exists.
Not found verbatim in Augustine. Loosely related to remarks in his Expositions of the Psalms on singing and praise. Treat as unsourced.

misattributions.line: The floor of hell is paved with the skulls of priests (or bishops)
misattributions.truth: No source located in Chrysostom's works; widely repeated online without a reference. Treat as unsourced.
